:::{#exm-stationary-sequence}
#### A sticky coin
<!-- no-figure: the example is a short argument with no data to plot -->

Let $X_1$ be a fair coin toss, coded $0$ or $1$.
For each $t \ge 2$, let $X_t$ equal $X_{t-1}$ with [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $0.9$
and $1 - X_{t-1}$ with probability $0.1$,
independently of $X_1, \ldots, X_{t-2}$ given $X_{t-1}$.
If $X_{t-1}$ is fair, then so is $X_t$,
because

$$\P(X_t = 1) = 0.9 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} + 0.1 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2},$$

which is $1/2$.
So, by [induction](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/induction.html#def-proof-by-induction) on $t$, every $X_t$ is $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$.
The probability that $k$ consecutive tosses take given values
is then $1/2$ times $0.9$ for each repeat and $0.1$ for each switch.
That product does not depend on which toss the run starts at,
so the sticky coin is a [stationary sequence](#def-stationary-sequence).

:::
